newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish cabinet minister quits in Islamist row.
newsitem.headline: Turkish cabinet minister quits in Islamist row.

text.p: A Turkish minister resigned from the cabinet on Friday in a row over Islamist activism, dealing a a further setback to Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's wobbly coalition.
Tourism Minister Bahattin Yucel told a news conference he had quit because the government's Islamist leanings put it at odds with Turkey's decades-old secularist tradition.
"I felt that it went against my parliamentary oath to stay in power, with the contradictions to our country's values that were involved," he said.
Yucel had been quoted in the Turkish press as urging Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, leader of his secularist True Path Party, to immediately pull out of the ruling alliance.
Pressure from the secularist army has brought the coalition close to collapse and a government plan to set up a caretaker administration to take the country to early polls has run into trouble.
But a leading True Path member said that the coalition partners had agreed to hand over the premiership from Erbakan to Ciller on June 18 as part of the run-up to early polls.
Hasan Ekinci, deputy chairman of Ciller's True Path Party, said on the private ATV channel on Thursday night that an announcement on the handover would be made on June 17.
Any power transfer would need to be approved by the president and parliament, where the year-old coalition now lacks a majority.
Erbakan's hopes of a boosted majority in parliament were dashed on Friday when a right-wing powerbroker said he would not join the planned caretaker government.
"We do not want to enter a government which is going to an election," Muhsin Yazicioglu, leader of the Grand Unity Party, said.
Yazicioglu, whose far-right party has eight MPs, had been negotiating with the alliance to become a third coalition partner.

The coalition has 274 MPs in the 550-seat assembly, with two seats vacant. Yazicioglu said his party was as yet undecided on whether to back the government in parliament, without actually joining the coalition.
